articles.title: Meta-Optimized Continual Adaptation for sustainable aquaculture monitoring systems for low-power autonomous deployments
articles.excerpt: Meta-Optimized Continual Adaptation for sustainable aquaculture monitoring systems for low-power autonomous deployments Introduction: A Pond, a Battery, and a Lesson in Humility Last spring, I spent t…
articles.body: Meta-Optimized Continual Adaptation for sustainable aquaculture monitoring systems for low-power autonomous deployments Introduction: A Pond, a Battery, and a Lesson in Humility Last spring, I spent three weekends at a small tilapia farm run by a friend's family, helping them retrofit a handful of solar-powered sensor buoys. The plan sounded trivial: log dissolved oxygen, temperature, and turbidity every few minutes, push the data over LoRaWAN, and flag anomalies. What could go wrong? Everything, as it turns out. The dissolved oxygen sensor drifted within days as biofilm accumulated on its membrane. A seasonal algae bloom shifted the entire statistical distribution of turbidity readings, so my carefully tuned anomaly detector started screaming false alarms at 3 a.m.

articles.title: What a weekly release rhythm looks like with a remote developer
articles.excerpt: Originally published on shipfastdev.com. When you hire a remote developer, the hardest part isn’t the code. It’s knowing what is happening between two calls. A fixed weekly rhythm answers that questio…
articles.body: Originally published on shipfastdev.com . When you hire a remote developer, the hardest part isn’t the code. It’s knowing what is happening between two calls. A fixed weekly rhythm answers that question before you have to ask it. Monday: agree the week’s goals The week starts with a short call. You and your developer agree what should be live by Friday: a feature, a set of bug fixes, or a step towards a larger release. Anything too big for one week is split into pieces that each work on their own. Midweek: a preview link Halfway through the week you get a link to try what’s in progress. You click through it like a user would, and you say what feels wrong while it is still cheap to change.

articles.title: Customer-Support Knowledge Base Crawl Boundaries: Lower Index Cost, Traceable Retrieval
articles.excerpt: Short answer: use a staged retrieval design with explicit collections, bounded queries, and traceable source context. For a fintech support knowledge base, the least complex option is a narrow crawl c…
articles.body: Short answer: use a staged retrieval design with explicit collections, bounded queries, and traceable source context. For a fintech support knowledge base, the least complex option is a narrow crawl contract: index only approved help content, preserve tenant and access metadata on every item, and make ingestion, retrieval, and citation separate observable stages. The page that wakes the on-call is usually not the crawler. It is a support answer that cites an old fee schedule, or an answer that quietly mixes one tenant's policy with another's. By the time that page fires, index growth and missing telemetry have already made the incident expensive. I would start from the answer the customer is allowed to see and work backwards to a retrieval contract.

articles.title: Reading your team's Git history as a manager, without leaving VS Code
articles.excerpt: I'm Pavel, the founder of DevGhost. This post walks through what I built it for: an engineering lead who lives in VS Code and wants to understand what their team's Git history says about the work behi…
articles.body: I'm Pavel, the founder of DevGhost. This post walks through what I built it for: an engineering lead who lives in VS Code and wants to understand what their team's Git history says about the work behind it. Commit counts and lines of code don't answer that. A one-line fix can take a day; a generated migration can add 2,000 lines in a minute. So DevGhost estimates something else. The baseline For every change, DevGhost estimates how long it would take a reference developer: mid-level, familiar with the codebase, working without AI. That gives every person and every period the same yardstick. Two numbers come out of it: Contribution, h : estimated reference-developer hours behind the changes. Not time actually worked.

articles.title: 6 Clauses Your Freelance Contract Needs (Or You Risk Not Getting Paid)
articles.excerpt: I built a free contract checklist tool that scans a pasted contract for missing clauses. Writing the checks made it obvious which 6 clauses actually matter — the rest is boilerplate. "Build a website"…
articles.body: I built a free contract checklist tool that scans a pasted contract for missing clauses. Writing the checks made it obvious which 6 clauses actually matter — the rest is boilerplate. 1. Scope and acceptance criteria "Build a website" is a conversation topic, not a scope. Name the exact deliverable, format, and how the client verifies it is done. Without this, every revision request becomes an unwinnable argument about what you actually promised. 2. Acceptance deadline with an auto-accept clause Give the client a fixed number of days (3-5 business days is typical) to approve the work or send written feedback. State that silence past the deadline counts as acceptance.

articles.body: On Oct. 17, 2016, Orbital ATK (now Northrop Grumman Space Systems ) returned to flight, successfully launching a cargo shipment to the International Space Station (ISS) after its previous cargo mission failed to launch. The private spaceflight company was contracted by NASA to fly cargo to the ISS, and stakes were high for this launch. Orbital ATK's last attempt nearly two years earlier ended in a catastrophic explosion a few seconds after liftoff. Despite some delays, the newly upgraded Antares rocket flawlessly blasted off into the night sky from NASA's Wallops Flight Facility in Virginia. Six days later, the Cygnus cargo spacecraft arrived at the ISS to deliver food, supplies and science experiments to the crew.

articles.title: The Orionid meteor shower peaks next week! Here's what to expect
articles.excerpt: The Orionid meteor shower peaks overnight on Oct. 21-22, bringing a spectacular display of shooting stars to the autumn sky.
articles.body: The Orionid meteor shower peaks overnight on Oct. 21-22, triggering a spectacular display of shooting stars as Earth plunges through the densest part of the debris trail shed by Halley's Comet. Here's what you need to know. When is the best time to see Orionid shooting stars? Orionid meteors are best spotted between the hours of midnight and dawn on Oct. 22, when 10-20 shooting stars may be seen brightening the night sky each hour under ideal dark-sky. The glare cast by the 74%-lit waxing gibbous moon will hide fainter shooting stars for much of the night. Thankfully, the lunar disk will set a few hours after midnight, leaving a window of beautifully dark sky before dawn in which to enjoy the full majesty of the annual meteor shower.

articles.excerpt: The actions could have resulted in criminal charges had humans been behind the keyboard.
articles.body: OpenAI said internal models hacked two more websites, bypassed company-imposed browsing restrictions, and used exposed credentials to draw cryptocurrency from a wallet it couldn’t otherwise access, in the latest installment of disclosures of its agents performing unethical and likely illegal acts. The company on Thursday issued reports of four new incidents, all of which occurred in June. They come after the company revealed in July that internal test agents exploited a zero-day vulnerability in a tool designed to restrict their access to the Internet. They then broke into the network of AI tool provider Hugging Face. The agents took that illegal action to steal answers to a hacking test that weren’t available when completing the tasks on their own.
